slides.0.title: Quebec and Other Provinces
slides.0.subtitle: Quebec's cold-hardy grapes and winter protection, and a comparison of provincial scale
slides.1.title: Quebec's history
slides.1.highlights.0.title: From Champlain to Prohibition
slides.1.highlights.0.content: In 1608 Samuel de Champlain planted European vines that did not survive the winter; in 1919 Quebec enacted total prohibition but a later provincial vote excluded beer, wine and cider, so it was the sole region of North America to escape total prohibition (Wikipedia)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: The SAQ monopoly
slides.1.highlights.1.content: The Commission des liqueurs du Québec, created in 1921, later became the Société des alcools du Québec (SAQ), which holds a legal monopoly on alcohol distribution (Wikipedia)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: The modern industry
slides.1.highlights.2.content: The Association des vignerons du Québec formed in 1987 and was renamed the Conseil des vins du Québec in 2018; Domaine des Côtes d'Ardoise, opened in 1979, is the oldest vineyard still operating, and most vineyards were planted in the 1980s (Wikipedia, Luxe Magazine)
slides.1.content: Quebec's wine industry is young, but its winemaking roots are early.
slides.2.title: Cold-hardy grapes and winter protection
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Cold-hardy hybrids
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Common varieties include Frontenac (noir, gris, blanc), Vidal, Seyval Blanc and Maréchal Foch; cold-hardy varieties from the University of Minnesota were bred to survive down to -40°C. Reds include Maréchal Foch, Frontenac, De Chaunac and Sainte-Croix; whites include Vidal, Seyval Blanc and L'Acadie Blanc (Luxe Magazine, Wikipedia)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Winter protection
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Some wineries bury their vines, and growers increasingly cover vineyards with geotextile coverings to shield them from cold (Luxe Magazine)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Little vinifera
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Vinifera varieties such as Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Riesling make up less than 10% of acreage (Luxe Magazine)
slides.2.content: Quebec relies on cold-hardy hybrids and winter protection.
slides.3.title: Rules, styles and provincial scale
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Vin du Québec PGI
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Since 2018 the Vin du Québec PGI guarantees 100% Quebec grapes from a defined region, and wines must pass a tasting panel (Luxe Magazine). The number of regions is given as 6, 7 or 9, and winery and acreage figures also differ, so none is tested
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Ice cider and styles
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Luxe Magazine credits Christian Barthomeuf of Clos Saragnat with creating ice cider; wine styles cover white, rosé, red, fortified, sweet and sparkling (including traditional method and pét-nat)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Provincial scale
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Areas cited by Vins du Québec: Canada totals more than 12,000 ha; Ontario 6,879 ha (53%), BC 4,152 ha (33%), Quebec about 1,000 ha (8%) and Nova Scotia 400 ha (3%); Quebec wine sales in 2023 were 2.25 million litres, down 5% on the year
slides.3.content: Ontario and BC together hold over 80% of Canada's vineyards.
